explanation: Fires mostly on words in prose about social, medical or behavioural problems and risks, either naming the problem or sitting inside the phrase about it (corruption, dependence, gambling, unintended pregnancies, recurrence, accident, spread of infection, hatred and violence). There are also scattered high hits on numbers and function words with no clear link to this, and neutral prose gives weak activation.

Fires on the first token of a word in non-English text written in Latin or Cyrillic script (Italian, Romanian, Portuguese, Danish, Norwegian, Russian, Estonian, Indonesian and others), most strongly on function words or word-initial pieces just after punctuation. Foreign personal names and word fragments inside English text give moderate-to-weak activation; ordinary English gives almost none.

Fires mainly on structural tokens in source code and markup: tokens right after a blank line or a closing brace (namespace, import, var logger, $provide), stack-trace 'at', and URL or path pieces. It also fires fairly strongly on some ordinary news-prose tokens ('the', 'at least', 'to'), so it is a mixture.

Fires on the modifier word of a technical compound noun in technical or patent-style prose (power requirements, metal oxide, neural tube, side platform, wireless device, cable railing, fee-for-service). It also fires on CJK characters in localization strings and on number punctuation in statistics.

Fires on the unit or determiner inside time and distance expressions, especially 'years' in 'X years ago', 'days ago', 'a year later', 'this week', 'X miles'. It also fires on 'how', 'just' and 'so' introducing a clause or modifier ('texting me how am I', 'just south of'). The time-expression job is the strongest.

Mixture: Russian-language text inside programming Q&A or code (prepositions and words such as к, в, на, наши), the hyphen before shell 'find' flags, the digits of copyright years in code headers, the prefix 'mis', and various technical tokens.

Fires on tokens in prose about political geography and international affairs: names of nations, ethnic groups and regions, and words in phrases about states, coalitions, elections and borders (nine Arab states, Slavic Wagrians, Pakistan Peoples Party, National Assembly, secession from Sudan). Sports and other prose with regional names gives weaker activation.

Fires on words that frame a group, collection or set of things, usually in 'X of' constructions or plural or set nouns: 'list of', 'one or several', 'a complex of', 'course of', 'a number of', 'string of', 'array', 'plural', 'layers', 'team', 'bunch'. The token itself and the 'collection' reading both matter.

Fires on programming code and coding-help prose, strongest on comment markers or words that open a comment or an explanation (# TODO, //, 'You may find', 'You might want to try', 'def', indentation at the start of a function body). Non-programming text gives at most weak activation.

Mixture of formatting tokens: whitespace and indentation runs in code or config, '::' in C++, broken multibyte CJK/Devanagari/Greek bytes, spaces before version numbers or postcodes, and some ordinary prose tokens ('right to', 'a degree').

Mixture with no shared theme: '$' inside bcrypt hashes, the minus sign starting a new equation after a comma in algebra problems, 'pro se' in legal text, string literals in JavaScript/PHP code, and assorted nouns ('private key', 'breech presentation', 'Coupon Code', 'regular season').

Fires inside license and copyright boilerplate at the top of source files: comment markers ('//', ' *'), Go '// +build' tags, '://' in license URLs, and words of the license text. Strongest on the comment-marker or '+' token that starts a line in such a header; ordinary code or prose URLs give weaker activation.

Two loosely related jobs: tokens inside math expressions or problems (numbers, sin, limits, derivatives) and biomedical terms, especially diabetes and insulin vocabulary (β-cell, insulin, beta cells, prognostic). There is also scattered weaker activation in code and prose.

Fires strongly across very varied tokens with no clear common thread: Go/Kotlin code tokens (':=', 'data class'), the prefix 'ant'/'anti', 'data' in technical prose, prepositions ('for', 'of', 'against', 'in') and commas in abstracts, and possessives.
